tldr: Trandafir starts from an order method with too many side effects and walks through the dual-write problem, sagas (orchestration versus choreography), the transactional outbox and the inbox for idempotent consumers.
summary: Trandafir, a Java developer from Bucharest who writes for Baeldung, argues that the time AI saves on typing should go into observability and architecture. His running example is a placeOrder method in an e-commerce app that inserts an order, updates products, publishes a Kafka domain event, writes a file, POSTs to a loyalty service and sends an email. A test full of mocks is the hint that the design is wrong: none of these side effects can be made atomic together. This is the dual-write problem, and it applies even to writing to two databases.

The first answer is undoing work. If inventory fails after an OrderCreated event, it can publish StockUnavailable so the order service runs an idempotent compensating action (cancel the order). That is the saga pattern, as Chris Richardson defines it: a sequence of local transactions with compensations. Choreography (services react to each other's domain events) evolves quickly but makes error handling harder and couples services in both directions. Orchestration (a coordinator sends commands such as CreateOrder) keeps the workflow and rollback logic in one place, but moves all coupling into the orchestrator. Trandafir suggests mixing both, with choreographed parts talking to orchestrated parts only through the orchestrator, or using a modular monolith with Spring Modulith.

A live demo showed why wrapping a database write and a remote call in one transaction is dangerous. With a 1-second delay on the loyalty service, the POST endpoint used up the connection pool, and plain GET requests that only read from the database slowed down too. There is also a correctness gap: the Kafka message can already be out when the commit later fails on a constraint. Skipping the transaction gives at-most-once delivery, which is fine for promotional messages. Exactly-once does not exist, so for his earlier work in financial markets he aimed for at-least-once.

The transactional outbox writes the event to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the order. A poller or CDC process publishes it and marks it as processed. The relay can still produce duplicates, so each row carries an idempotency key and an observed-at timestamp as message headers. On the consumer side, the inbox pattern stores incoming messages in a table with a unique constraint on that key. When the constraint rejects a duplicate, the consumer acknowledges the message instead of failing. It also reorders messages within a time window by observed-at and separates retriable from non-retriable failures. In Q&A he noted that Kafka transactions still leave two commits that can diverge.
keyPoints: The dual-write problem: you cannot atomically change a database and a broker, an HTTP service, a file system or even a second database.
A test with many mocks that only verifies interactions is a sign that the method has too many side effects.
Sagas undo work with compensating actions, and those actions must be idempotent so they can be retried.

Orchestration centralises the workflow and error handling but concentrates coupling: every new service means changing and redeploying the orchestrator. Choreography lets you add a service by subscribing it to an existing channel.
Demo: making an external call 1 s slower inside a @Transactional method used up the connection pool and slowed unrelated GET endpoints.

The outbox gives at-least-once delivery with some extra latency. Use it when no message may be lost and reliability matters more than throughput. Spring Modulith supports it out of the box with a single table that stores the payload as a blob.
Inbox: put a unique constraint on the idempotency key, acknowledge rather than retry on constraint violations, and reorder by an observed-at header within a time window.
You don't need an inbox if the consumer is naturally idempotent, for example when it can deduplicate on business fields. Consider retry topics and dead-letter queues as well.
takeaways: Move remote calls and message publishing out of database transactions, and check the connection-acquire time in your metrics.
Use a transactional outbox, for example through Spring Modulith, for events you cannot afford to lose.
Attach an idempotency key and an observed-at timestamp to every published event so consumers can deduplicate and reorder.
Make compensating actions and consumers idempotent before adding sagas.
Use orchestration only for workflows that need reliable rollback, and choreography for the rest.

quotes.text: There is no such thing as exactly-once message delivery.
All the coupling just moved to the right-hand side, to the orchestrator.

watchIf: You publish domain events from a service that also writes to a database, and want a clear, pattern-by-pattern guide to keeping both consistent.
